message: I think Nels' post is helpful, and points to possible solutions.  Solutions come from an attitude of openness to other ways of thinking, of seeking first to understand. When I was in the Peace Corps, the people on my island told me that the volunteers who learned the language, and observed the cultural mores, touched the hearts and minds of those around them.  They made a difference and left a legacy.  The volunteers who kept to themselves, not bothering to learn or respect the culture, came and went, and were forgotten except for their unwillingness to become a part of the community.  I do have trouble with the statement that corruption is inherent in the Afghan culture.  (It seems to be inherent in our own culture, too!)  Is there a more useful way to characterize their culture that might lead to solutions?  For example, if you frame it as being strongly tied to a clan system, one could focus efforts towards change on the powerful clans, and the more moderate leaders of those clans.  Again, Nels' comment, and the experience of Greg Mortenson are helpful.  (Have you read Three Cups of Tea, Mortenson's first book?)  I like your blog.
